title: Report on Exchange Studies at Duke University and Stanford University
paragraphs: I was given the opportunity to take part in clinical clerkships for a little less than two months at Duke University and Stanford University in the United States. Both are universities with world-class reputations in both clinical practice and research, and being able to learn in those actual settings was a very valuable experience for me.

My reason for aspiring to this study abroad was that I wanted to broaden my horizons by learning at Duke University and Stanford University, which boast world-top-level clinical and research environments, and to picture my future image as a doctor more concretely. I am aiming to become a physician-scientist who can contribute to patients through both clinical practice and basic research, and in order to get closer to that ideal, I wanted to see and learn on site from the doctors working on the front line. What I am especially interested in is the field of neurosurgery, and within it research on brain tumors, including glioblastoma. I currently belong to the Department of Tumor Biology at Nagoya University and work on basic research on brain tumors. Given this background, I was also interested in brain tumor research overseas. At Duke University, research on immunotherapy and on targeting the tumor microenvironment for brain tumors is active. At Stanford University too there are labs working on similar themes, and many physician-scientists active worldwide in the fields of stroke and brain tumors are on the faculty. I felt that being able to learn in such an environment was attractive when thinking about my future. In addition, I myself have accumulated overseas experiences until now, such as medical English classes, overseas partnership programs, short-term clinical externships, and activities as a Visiting Student Researcher and Clinical Observer at Stanford Neurosurgery, but because these were mainly done before the sixth year, the hospital clerkships were mainly observation, and I could not become deeply involved with the medical team. This time, as a sixth-year student, I felt great significance in being able to access patients' charts and be involved in clinical care more practically, in the same position as local medical students. My wish to test how far my experience and learning until now would hold up in actual American medical settings also pushed me toward this study abroad.

At Stanford University, I did my clerkship in neuroradiology (Neuroradiology). In the reading room, I presented to the resident the cases I had read beforehand and confirmed the final findings under the guidance of the attending physician. In addition, I attended Neuroradiology lectures, case conferences and joint conferences with Neurosurgery. On the last day of the clerkship, I gave a PowerPoint presentation on a case that interested me, which was an opportunity to organize what I had learned. During the clerkship I also observed neurointerventional radiology (Neurointerventional Radiology), and I was also able to attend the operations of a doctor who is a world-renowned physician-scientist, who developed stem cell therapy after stroke from basic research to clinical application, and who also works as a neurosurgeon, including bypass surgery for moyamoya disease.

What I had been interested in even before the clerkship was the use of the perfusion imaging analysis system (CT Perfusion) in acute ischemic stroke. While its introduction in Japan is limited, in the United States it is actively used to decide treatment policy, and it was a valuable opportunity to learn directly from the doctors on site about its advantages and challenges and how they actually use it in diagnosis. In particular, Stanford is the institution that led the "DEFUSE 3 trial," which attracted worldwide attention. In this trial, by quantitatively evaluating the ischemic core and penumbra using CT perfusion imaging, thrombectomy was shown to be effective even for acute ischemic stroke patients 6 to 16 hours after onset, and it was published in NEJM. It was a very valuable experience to learn at the institution of this trial, which overturned the conventional wisdom of the "within 6 hours" treatment window and brought great change to clinical practice. Also, among the supervising doctors, some introduced actual cases in which CT perfusion imaging contributed greatly to diagnosis, which was very interesting. In addition, regarding "W-EB," a device for embolization of aneurysms in neurointerventional therapy, its clinical introduction in Japan had only recently begun, so it was very interesting to hear directly the opinions of American doctors who already have a lot of experience with many cases.

Interacting with a different attending physician each day of the week, I was able to touch on each doctor's different way of thinking and viewpoint in diagnosis. They explained carefully in response to questions, and sometimes pulled up images from their own past cases to explain. In particular, at the case presentation on the last day I was able to discuss with the doctors things I had been wondering about, and it was a meaningful time.

At Duke University, I joined the Hematology-Oncology team as a Sub-intern and gained very practical and stimulating clinical experience. In the first, second and fourth weeks I belonged to the hematologic malignancy ward team, and in the third week to the solid tumor consult team, and I practiced the series of tasks of chart review, history taking, physical examination, presentation, order entry and chart writing while taking charge of two patients. I checked my assigned patients' information after receiving handover from the night team, and on rounds I reported the key points of what had happened since the previous day's rounds and proposed that day's management plan for the remaining problems. Contributing as a member of an actual medical team, such as performing physical examinations and explaining test results and the day's schedule to patients, was very valuable. It was also a very meaningful experience to be in charge of patients in an English environment and to experience a setting where clinical practice, research and education are closely linked.

At Duke, many doctors are actively involved in clinical trials, and many patients were seen participating in new trials. The atmosphere of the setting where daily care and clinical research are closely linked was very impressive, and I realized that medicine is always at the forefront of evolution. In the clinical setting, I also received careful guidance on the approach to the differential diagnosis of diseases and treatment strategies during rounds, which was a valuable opportunity to cultivate practical clinical thinking. In particular, in the rounds I experienced the style in which the whole team went carefully through eight patients one by one over nearly three hours in the morning, and I was surprised at the difference from rounds in Japan. On the other hand, lectures were relatively compact at about 30 minutes, and rather than detailed explanations of pathophysiology, they were often taught from the viewpoint of how treatment has changed, based on graphs of trial results and evidence, and I felt the difference in educational style.

What was especially memorable was shadowing the Neuro-oncology (brain tumor) clinic. (As a Hematology-Oncology Sub-intern, after finishing the morning rounds and chart writing, the work was basically only accompanying the residents to examine new inpatients, and students were not required to take part. For that reason, I devoted the afternoon time to fields I was interested in.) Duke puts great effort into brain tumor research, and when I shadowed, there were 13 trials ongoing for high grade glioma alone. Among them, many innovative efforts were under way, such as the modified poliovirus for recurrent glioblastoma (studied in Duke's basic research laboratories and actually brought to clinical trial) and a trial of an IDH inhibitor combined with an immune checkpoint inhibitor, and I could see up close how basic research and clinical practice work closely together.

In that setting I also had the opportunity to sit in on a consultation with a patient. It was a person with glioblastoma that had recurred in multiple places, for whom a specific CAR-T therapy (because there was no mutation to serve as the target molecule) and the modified poliovirus therapy (because of multiple-site recurrence) were not indicated, and what was very impressive was the neuro-oncologist carefully offering the patient and family treatment options (other CAR-T trials, standard treatments and so on). Witnessing that reality, I strongly felt the limits of glioblastoma treatment at present and the importance of research and clinical trials to provide better treatment options, and it was also an event that made me strongly want, in the future, to work putting effort into research too, for such patients someday.

Through the clerkships I learned how proactively American medical students act within actual team medicine. For the patients I was in charge of, I was expected to make treatment proposals based on the test results, and I was given the chance to apply in the field the knowledge I had learned in lectures. Also, there were many doctors who combine clinical work and research, and some limit clinical work to only a few weeks a year and devote the rest to research, and it left an impression that each builds a career while devising how to use their own time.

What impressed me was how very active Stanford medical students are in taking part in research. Classes are mainly on-demand, lectures are watched at home, and they spend the daytime on research in labs and extracurricular activities, so a flexible way of learning suited to one's own style has taken hold. Studying medicine is taken for granted, and I was greatly stimulated by their attitude of also actively engaging in research and social activities on top of that. In the United States, experience in basic research is often required even before entering medical school, and students aiming especially at academic university medical schools devote themselves actively to research from high school and undergraduate days. I felt that this background leads to medical students' high research orientation and initiative.

The role of medical students in clinical clerkships is also very different from Japan. In the United States, the system is such that one begins residency in the desired specialty immediately after graduating from medical school, so a high level of clinical participation is required even from the student stage. They took charge of one to three patients and did everything from daily rounds, presentations, orders for tests and drugs, to explanations to patients, in effect playing a role close to that of initial residents in Japan. What was especially impressive is that even medical students are asked to propose treatment plans, and these are actually discussed and adopted within the team. There is a culture of asking for opinions regardless of one's position as a student, and I strongly felt the attitude that education is not one-way but always dialogical and participatory. Feedback was also given frequently, and I found the educational environment, which deepens learning on the spot, very attractive.

Furthermore, in every department there is a lecture once a week called "Grand Rounds," for which renowned experts in the field are invited from outside the school, providing an opportunity to learn the latest research results and clinical knowledge. I was also impressed that such continuous learning opportunities function as a mechanism that further raises professional expertise as a healthcare worker.

During my stay at Stanford, I had many opportunities to talk directly with Japanese doctors and hear about the medical systems of Japan and the United States, career building, lifestyle and so on. In the field of neurosurgery, I interacted with doctors who are active as faculty after fellowships and with doctors engaged in research study abroad, and was able to hear about their backgrounds for going to the United States and their future prospects. In addition, through the kindness of a Japanese doctor in transplant surgery, I was allowed to take part in lectures and rounds for surgery faculty and residents. I was also allowed to join several other doctors for meals, and I am filled with gratitude for their warm welcome.

I also visited the lab of Dr. 岡田, who does brain tumor immunology research, at UCSF near Stanford, and interacted with Japanese researchers studying abroad. Meeting people of diverse backgrounds, such as doctors from the Nagoya University neurosurgery department, a German neurosurgery resident, and a student technical assistant aiming to enter medical school in the United States, was very stimulating. I also took part in a lab meeting of a laboratory that had looked after me previously at Stanford, and interacted with medical students and clerkship students from other countries, and it was a fruitful time.

During my stay at Duke, I visited UNC (University of North Carolina), and Dr. Larson, who came to the program held at Nagoya University last summer, showed me around the hospital, departments and simulation center. I was also able to learn about the differences between UNC and Duke, the fields each university focuses on, and how doctors work. I also toured the campus with Ray, a UNC student who had studied at Nagoya University, and other students, and by chance met and talked with a Japanese UNC medical student with connections to Nagoya University. Furthermore, I met Dr. Gordon of Duke, who came to Nagoya University last summer, and was given the opportunity to observe the emergency department on a Sunday.

During my stay I was warmly welcomed by my homestay hosts Fred and Jenny, who were very kind to me, taking me out to dinner and so on. In addition, I was taken to tourist sights by Dr. 長谷川 and his wife, who graduated from Nagoya University about 20 years ago, experienced a clerkship in the United States in their sixth year, and now do research at UNC, and I also met Dr. 原田 and his family, who did a clerkship at Duke as a student and is still active in the United States, and was taken out to meals. At the social gathering that Dr. 原田 organized, I was also able to interact with Japanese doctors doing basic research at Duke and UNC.

After the clerkship at Duke, I took part in AANS (American Association of Neurological Surgeons), the largest neurosurgery conference in the United States, held in Boston. I had wanted to attend this conference since the stage of applying internally for Duke, and I had submitted an abstract to this conference around autumn last year and it had been accepted as an e-poster, so I attended as a presenter. AANS is held every year at the end of April or the beginning of May, and this year, luckily, it was held in Boston, just after my clerkship at Duke ended. It was very interesting to listen to lectures by doctors whom I admire as a woman neurosurgeon who also puts effort into research, to attend sessions I was interested in, and to learn the latest knowledge and research in the field of neurosurgery.

During my stay in Boston I was also able to meet Dr. 布施, a Nagoya University graduate who is studying for one year at the Harvard MPH (School of Public Health), Japanese doctors enrolled in the MPH through his network, Dr. David, a neuro-oncology specialist doing brain tumor research at MGH (Massachusetts General Hospital) (a doctor from the Medical University of Vienna who did an exchange clerkship at Nagoya University as a student), and a Japanese woman neurosurgeon doing research study abroad on brain tumors. I was also allowed to visit the brain tumor research lab at MGH, and was able to learn about the path to establishing a lab in the United States and the American research environment.

Looking back, during this stay I was blessed with opportunities to meet many doctors and students with connections to Nagoya University. That I could meet and connect with so many doctors and have such valuable experiences is thanks to the international network that Nagoya University has built over many years. This experience, gained while being warmly supported by many people, has become a treasure for me that nothing can replace. I am sincerely grateful to have been given such encounters and experiences.

The two months of clinical clerkships in the United States were a very valuable experience when thinking about my future career. What left the greatest impression was the following words I received from a professor who has long served as an attending at Duke. "Your presentations and treatment plans for your assigned patients have been excellent, which clearly shows you have the ability. I think you can contribute even more by sharing your thoughts during discussions about other patients as well, even when I am talking with the resident about their patients' cases. Don't hesitate to suggest plans or differentials. Your input is valuable, and you should be confident in what you bring." I was truly happy that he recognized my ability even though I am a medical student and encouraged me that "you can contribute more," and it led to great confidence. By placing myself in an environment where even students are expected to take part actively in discussions as members of the care team, I also had an opportunity to reconsider how I engage. By actually being asked for my opinion and being able to contribute to the team, I learned the importance of one's attitude toward clinical practice and of asserting oneself, and was able to realize the significance of speaking with confidence.

In addition, the many doctors I met through the clerkships, especially the physician-scientists who combine clinical practice and basic research, were a great stimulus for me. For example, in Duke's Neuro-oncology team, of nine clinicians, three run basic research labs, and I felt that balancing a lab and clinical practice is not common even in the United States and requires drive. On the other hand, among the Stanford Neurosurgery faculty, there were many doctors with basic research labs, and I got the impression that a culture that values research is more deeply rooted. In fact, many Stanford medical students said "I chose this medical school because I want to do research," and I was greatly stimulated by their attitude. In the United States, the general system is that after graduating from medical school one goes through residency, deepens one's specialty in a fellowship, and then steps up from assistant professor to associate professor to professor, but I heard that the earliest people sometimes set up their own labs immediately after finishing a fellowship.

I too aim in the future to become a physician-scientist active on both the clinical and research axes. This time, by being able to talk directly with doctors who are actually walking that path and with young doctors who are about to go down it, my image of my goal became clearer. Their figures have become role models for me, and the strong feeling that "someday I want to be like this" has arisen, which is the greatest harvest I gained from studying abroad.

Through this training I experienced the differences in medicine, education and culture between Japan and the United States and was blessed with encounters with many wonderful people. Through this experience, the image of the doctor I aim to be became more concrete, and my wish to contribute to society in the future through both clinical practice and research has grown stronger.

Finally, I sincerely thank all the doctors and everyone who supported this valuable study abroad opportunity. First of all, I would like to express my deep gratitude to the staff of the International Collaboration Office, starting with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, who gave great support from the preparation stage, to Dr. Itzel, who has carefully taught me medical English since my early years, and to the doctors who looked after me in the pre-departure study abroad training. I also sincerely thank the Keiichi Shibahara Fund (柴原慶一基金), which supported this study abroad financially. In addition, I sincerely thank the people of the international offices of Duke University and Stanford University who warmly accepted me for the clerkships, the many doctors who instructed me during the clerkships, Jenny and Fred, who welcomed me warmly at my homestay, the doctors and students who took precious time to meet me during my stay in the United States, and the doctors who introduced me to people on site. I also realize anew that a clerkship like this one was possible only through the efforts of everyone who has supported Nagoya University's international collaboration over many years. I would like to take this opportunity to thank you once again. Thank you very much.
